texts.x: UPSC Syllabus: Gs Paper 2- Government policies and interventions for development in various sectors and issues arising out of their design and implementation. Introduction The Forest Rights Act (FRA), 2006, has strengthened land and livelihood rights of millions of tribal and forest-dwelling communities. Yet, recognised rights do not ensure secure incomes or productive land use.…
While the Forest Rights Act (FRA), 2006, has strengthened land and livelihood rights of millions of tribals and forest-dwelling communities, the next step is to complement these rights

points: The Forest Rights Act, 2006 has granted millions of tribal and forest-dwelling families legal rights over land, but titles alone do not provide livelihoods.
Authors propose growing pulses and oilseeds on FRA plots to turn titles into productive assets and reduce India's import dependence.
Pulses and oilseeds are ideal because they adapt to rain-fed and marginal lands, raise productivity, and foster climate-resilient farming.
An FAO-based soil analysis shows that out of 244 tribal districts, 60 have oilseed potential, 31 have pulse potential, and 23 favor both.
Current challenges include a 47 percent approval rate for individual FRA claims, a heavy wheat-rice bias in procurement, and cheap edible oil imports.
Proposed solutions include region-specific clusters, inputs, watershed management, local storage, farmer producer organisations, and GIS-based planning.
The strategy can converge with existing schemes like PM Krishi Sinchayee Yojana, National Mission on Edible Oils, and PM-AASHA.
Targeting aspirational districts helps direct development efforts to regions lagging on key social and economic indicators.
sum.text:
The Forest Rights Act, 2006 (FRA) has given millions of tribal and forest-dwelling families legal rights over land. Two authors now propose growing pulses and oilseeds on these plots to turn titles into livelihoods, because these crops suit rain fed marginal land and could cut India’s import dependence.
FRA lands: The Act recognises land rights of Scheduled Tribes and other forest dwellers who long occupied forest land. A title without seed, water and a market is like a shop licence without stock.
Next step: A parcel of land is the base of a livelihood only if conditions make it productive and sustainable. The authors want titles paired with sustainable farming, soil and water management, institutional support and market access.
Why these crops: Pulses and oilseeds adapt to rain fed (watered only by rainfall) and marginal (poor quality) land, raise productivity and support climate-resilient farming. They also strengthen domestic supplies.
The takeaway: A title secures the land, but crops and support decide whether it becomes a livelihood.
Soil suitability: An analysis using the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) soil map finds many tribal regions suited to soybean, groundnut, sunflower, mustard, chickpea and other pulses.
Oilseeds: Of the 244 tribal districts, 60 have major oilseed production potential.
Pulses: 31 districts have strong pulse potential, and 23 have favourable conditions for both crops.
Cropping pattern: Paddy and maize dominate the Kharif (monsoon) season, and wheat, gram, mustard and lentil the Rabi (winter) season. Millets, cotton, sesame and spices offer scope for sustainable diversification.
Local variety: The districts span 33 States and Union Territories with different settlement patterns and resources, so plans must follow local conditions.
Scheme convergence: The authors would link the plan to the PM Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (irrigation), National Food Security and Nutrition Mission , National Mission on Edible Oils (edible oil output), PM-AASHA (price support) and Van Dhan Yojana (tribal produce).
Aspirational districts: Many tribal districts overlap with aspirational districts, the districts flagged as lagging on development indicators, so the effort reaches places with the greatest need.
Recognition gap: Only 47% of individual claims under the FRA have been approved, so many families hold no title to farm.
Wheat-rice bias: Procurement favours wheat and rice, so oilseeds and pulses lack assured markets that would reward…

points: India's Public Distribution System provides subsidised foodgrains to millions through nearly five lakh Fair Price Shops.
Geographically tied ration entitlements weakened beneficiary bargaining power and created heavy dependence on assigned dealers.
Breaking the dealer monopoly requires expanding beneficiary choice, strengthening accountability, and improving foodgrain delivery.
Historical challenges included leakage, corruption, storage inefficiencies, exclusion errors, and limited nutritional diversity beyond wheat and rice.
Reform measures like One Nation One Ration Card empower beneficiaries to switch dealers and collect rations anywhere via Aadhaar.
Digital initiatives such as SMART PDS, Anna Chakra, Depot Darpan, and AI-enabled innovations enhance transparency and efficiency.
Data shows portability is frequently used locally, with portable transactions in Bihar increasing by six percentage points annually.
Future steps involve strengthening portability awareness, improving dealer accountability, modernising storage, and promoting nutritional security through diversified items.
sum.text:
India’s Public Distribution System (PDS) provides subsidised foodgrains to millions through nearly 5 lakh Fair Price Shops (FPSs) . However, geographically tied ration entitlements weakened beneficiaries’ bargaining power and made them dependent on assigned dealers. Breaking this monopoly requires expanding beneficiary choice, strengthening accountability and improving foodgrain delivery.
Origin of PDS: The PDS began as a wartime rationing measure during World War II and later expanded to address food shortages and ensure food security.
Expansion during the 1960s: The system expanded to address widespread food shortages, while the establishment of the Food Corporation of India (FCI) strengthened foodgrain procurement and storage.
Revamped Public Distribution System (1992): The RPDS was introduced to improve food distribution and extend coverage to remote and difficult areas.
Targeted Public Distribution System (1997): The TPDS classified households into Below Poverty Line (BPL) and Above Poverty Line (APL) categories to improve targeting of food subsidies.
Antyodaya Anna Yojana (2000): The scheme provided highly subsidised foodgrains to the poorest families, strengthening support for the most vulnerable households.
National Food Security Act (2013): The NFSA established a legal framework for subsidised foodgrain entitlements covering approximately 67% of India’s population , making food security a statutory entitlement.
Food Security: The PDS provides subsidised cereals to nearly 6 in 10 Indians every month, making it a major instrument of household food security.
Extensive Distribution Network: Nearly 5 lakh fair-price shops provide widespread access to subsidised foodgrains, supporting food distribution across the country.
Support for Vulnerable Households: Subsidised foodgrains help eligible households meet their basic food requirements and reduce their dependence on market-priced cereals.
Protection during Economic Disruptions: The 2020 lockdown exposed the importance of accessible food entitlements, as geographically restricted ration access created difficulties for migrant workers away from home.
Dealer Monopoly: Before portability reforms, beneficiaries depended on assigned FPS dealers, limiting their ability to switch shops when dissatisfied with prices, quantities, grain quality or services.

explain.headline: Indian Agriculture Faces a Polycrisis Driven by Climate and Energy Shocks
static: India’s agricultural sector contributes significantly to employment and raw material supply, but remains heavily dependent on the south-west monsoon for irrigation across large parts of cultivable land.
Chemical fertiliser usage in India expanded rapidly post-Green Revolution, with urea and complex fertilisers heavily subsidised by the government under nutrient-based and flat-rate subsidy regimes.
Biofuel policies in India, governed by the National Policy on Biofuels, aim to blend ethanol with petrol, incentivising the use of various feedstocks including sugarcane and surplus grains.
Agricultural credit and crop insurance frameworks, such as the Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY), are key institutional mechanisms designed to provide financial protection against crop losses.
Groundwater depletion in major agrarian states like Punjab, Haryana, and parts of southern India poses a severe sustainability challenge due to intensive power and pump subsidies.

explain.background: Modern Indian agriculture's heavy reliance on chemical inputs, imported raw materials, and fossil fuels makes it vulnerable to external geopolitical shocks and erratic monsoons.

Highlights the compounding threats of climate change, water scarcity, and food inflation on rural livelihoods and household security.
Emphasizes the urgent policy imperative to transition from short-term drought relief to long-term agricultural resilience.

texts.x: UPSC Syllabus: Gs Paper 3- Food Security Introduction Indian agriculture faces a polycrisis driven by geopolitical conflicts, weak monsoon, climate uncertainty, rising input costs and water scarcity. Its growing dependence on fossil fuels exposes farming to external energy shocks, while diversion of food crops towards biofuels creates food-fuel competition. At the same time, rainfall dependence…

points: Indian agriculture faces a polycrisis driven by geopolitical conflicts, weak monsoon, climate uncertainty, rising input costs, and water scarcity.
The fossilisation of farming is evident as India's tractor population crossed 1.2 crore and fertiliser consumption reached 33.5 million tonnes in 2025-26.
Heavy reliance on imported oil, gas, and fertiliser raw materials exposes Indian farming to severe external energy shocks and price volatility.
Geopolitical conflicts in West Asia and the Black Sea have spiked global input prices, raising landed sulphur prices in India to $1,000–1,100 per tonne.
High crude oil prices encourage the diversion of food crops like sugarcane, rice, and maize toward biofuels, intensifying food-fuel competition.
Climate uncertainty, weak monsoons, and a prospective El Nino increase crop losses, disrupt planning, and heighten agrarian distress and indebtedness.
Only one-third of urea's nitrogen is absorbed by crops, while three-fourths of DAP's phosphorus gets locked in the soil, showing inefficient nutrient use.
Policy recommendations include improving fertiliser efficiency, promoting biostimulants, strengthening water conservation, encouraging climate-resilient farming, and reforming agricultural markets.
sum.text:
Indian agriculture faces a polycrisis driven by geopolitical conflicts, weak monsoon, climate uncertainty, rising input costs and water scarcity. Its growing dependence on fossil fuels exposes farming to external energy shocks, while diversion of food crops towards biofuels creates food-fuel competition. At the same time, rainfall dependence threatens farm incomes and food affordability. These interconnected risks highlight the need to shift from short-term relief towards long-term agricultural resilience.
Fossilisation of Farming: India’s tractor population has crossed 1.2 crore, while fertiliser consumption reached 33.5 million tonnes of N, P and K in 2025-26. Urea and DAP accounted for around 67.5% of consumption, increasing dependence on chemical inputs.
Dependence on Imported Energy and Raw Materials: India imports oil, gas and fertiliser raw materials, including ammonia, rock phosphate, sulphur and muriate of potash. Many crop protection chemicals also depend on imported technical-grade ingredients and intermediates.
Geopolitical Conflicts and Input Price Shocks: Conflicts in West Asia and the Black Sea region have raised global input prices. LNG prices delivered to Northeast Asian markets rose from around $11 to $30 per million British thermal units, while sulphur’s landed price in India reached $1,000–1,100 per tonne.

points: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi presided over 46 petitions concerning anti-SIR protests and challenges to the Chief Election Commissioner.
Court 1 performed grand administrative stewardship by issuing notices, appointing nodal counsel, and ordering CCTV preservation, while leaving the ground reality static.
The author argues that centralising 40-odd time-sensitive civil liberties petitions into Court 1 created a bottleneck rather than providing immediate emergency relief.
In March 2023, a five-judge Constitution Bench in Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India ruled that the ECI selection committee must include the Prime Minister, Leader of the Opposition, and the CJI.
Parliament enacted the 2023 Act replacing the CJI with a Union cabinet minister, leading to the appointment of CEC Gyanesh Kumar under a contested law.
In Dr. Jaya Thakur v. Union of India, Justice Datta rejected executive control while Justice Sharma sought a reference to a five-judge bench under Article 145(3).
The ECI unilaterally modified Form 6 to require legacy citizenship and Aadhaar linkage, which the Court noted was not approved by it without granting a stay.
Section 16 of the 2023 Act grants serving and former Commissioners blanket statutory immunity from civil and criminal proceedings for official acts.
The Supreme Court prioritized long-term administrative docket management over immediate interim relief, leaving citizens waiting for substantive intervention.
sum.text:
In Samuel Beckett’s seminal absurdist play Waiting for Godot, two tramps, Vladimir and Estragon, stand beside a barren tree on a deserted country road, engaged in endless, highly structured dialogue while awaiting a mysterious figure who never arrives. They pace, they deliberate, they check their pocket watches. "Nothing happens, nobody comes, nobody goes, it's awful," Estragon famously laments..On the afternoon of October 15, as Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi rose after navigating 46 petitions related to the protests against the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, one could not help but sense a similar absurdist spectacle unfolding inside Court 1.
The Bench performed every motion of grand judicial stewardship. It issued notices, appointed nodal counsel, requested sealed covers and ordered law enforcement to preserve CCTV footage. Yet, beneath this flurry of administrative activity, the reality on the ground remained entirely static.
The SIR exercise rolls on, Jantar Mantar remains de-notified as a protest site and the executive secured the one currency it values above all else - time..To the seasoned court observer, the Bench’s approach carries a ready-made defence. Is it not standard practice for the master of the roster to centralise connected petitions to prevent contradictory orders across different benches? After all, since the street blockades and police actions were born out of the anti-SIR protests, shouldn't Court 1 hold the reins?
This argument sounds plausible, but it conflates two fundamentally distinct judicial duties - long-term constitutional adjudication and immediate, emergency relief..The writ petition challenging the validity of the SIR, filed by Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi and ten INDIA bloc leaders, rightfully belongs before the CJI. But the remaining 40-odd petitions concerned fundamental, time-sensitive civil liberties: lawyers allegedly battered while in police detention, journalists whose electronic equipment was confiscated and citizens detained under provisions like Section 172 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS). By retaining every single file under its own roof, Court 1 did not preserve order; it created a bottleneck.
Instead of allowing three or four independent division benches to immediately interrogate police excesses or issue protective orders, every emergency was funneled into a single,…

The executive's response relied on sweeping preventive measures, exposing a wide chasm between administrative reality and constitutional jurisprudence.
Authorities used Section 163 of the BNSS, 2023, successor to CrPC Section 144, to blanket New Delhi with prohibitory orders on October 10, 2026.
The mechanical application of Section 163 ignored the constitutional distinction between localized law and order and broader public order issues.
The Supreme Court criticized these actions using Lord Diplock’s sledgehammer analogy and highlighted failures under the proportionality test.

sum.text:
In 2026, India witnessed widespread protests that exposed systemic failures and raised serious questions about constitutional safeguards and the rule of law. The summer agitation against the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET-UG) irregularities and the autumn demonstrations revolving around the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and the demand for the Chief Election Commissioner's resignation highlighted a deeply concerning shift in the policing of democratic dissent.
The executive's response and its reliance on sweeping preventive measures expose a widening chasm between administrative reality and constitutional jurisprudence. The State’s response mechanism during these protests is Section 162 of the Bhartiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, the statutory successor to Section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), 1973. Despite the legislative transition, the colonial-era architecture of arbitrary spatial control remains intact. On October 10, 2026, the Delhi Police used Section 163 to blanket the New Delhi district, preemptively denying permission to protest, shutting down metro stations, cancelling trains, and imposing localised internet suspension. This mechanical application of Section 163 ignores the foundational constitutional distinction between “law and order” and “public order”.
The Supreme Court of India also expressed concern by applying Lord Diplock’s sledgehammer analogy. The Court questioned the executive's action based on the proportionality test. In the past, the Supreme Court has articulated, through the concentric circles doctrine in Ram Manohar Lohia v. State of Bihar (1965), that a disturbance to public order must possess a gravity affecting the broader community at large and invoke widespread panic. Traffic congestion or localised scuffles, frequently cited by authorities to deny permission to protest, are routine “law and order” issues that do not justify suspending rights conferred under Article 19(1)(b).
The Supreme Court, in the judgment Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020), has laid down the four-pronged proportionality test, and if we test the internet suspension and blanket bans, they fail the rigorous test. The Bhasin judgment explicitly mandated that executive orders must be tailored, necessary, and represent the least restrictive alternative. By routinely converting the fundamental right to assemble into a permission-based privilege and then persistently denying that permission,…

sum.text: China's tightening the tax net around its HNIs. Beijing levied a 20% I-T from offshore trusts in July, as well as on gains on assets moved into them, with a 90-day window to settle unpaid dues dating back to 2023. Tax offices in Beijing and Hangzhou have also begun taxing returns on offshore insurance policies. These aren't necessarily new taxes but stricter enforcement of existing taxes. Some also believe Beijing may introduce inheritance taxes. Developing economies often look to the US and China for cues on taxation, infra spending and policy. India, for one, must steer clear of emulating such tax policies. China's circumstances are materially different from India's. Its economy has slowed, and its government finances are under pressure. Its property market has endured prolonged stress, denying a key revenue source for local governments. Land sale revenue has had four straight years of double-digit decline. India's economy is expanding at a healthy pace, and housing is rising steadily. A policy that suits an economy grappling with a property bust can trigger different consequences in one still building its capital base. Capital is generally deployed more efficiently when it stays with individuals and enterprises that generated it. The state should retain what it needs for pivotal assets and essential revenue expenditure. The rupee, retained by a productive company, can fund a new factory, technology, research, hiring or expansion. Retained by a household, it becomes savings, investment or consumption. Each can set off another round of economic activity. The same rupee channelled through government can create significant value only when it goes into productive infrastructure. But this depends on the efficiency of deployment, which usually can't match the traction and momentum on the private side. This is not an argument against government spending. GoI has credibly done the heavy lifting by boosting capex when private investment was weak or selective. But rather than look for ways to enlarge GoI's share, India should focus on getting more output from every rupee it spends. Better focus, smart deployment and stronger outcomes should take precedence over raising taxes, or expanding recurring expenditure without corresponding productivity gains. Increasingly aggressive interpretation or enforcement of existing provisions can have unintended behavioural consequences. Businesses can become cautious about investing. Households may save and spend differently.…

sum.text:
The Supreme Court on Wednesday asked the Andhra Pradesh State Election Commission to defer publishing the final list of candidates for civic polls until October 25, news agency Press Trust of India reported. The court said, "Instilling confidence in the election process is vital for the maintenance of constitutional democracy."
A vacation bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana was hearing a petition filed by the Yuvajana Sramika Rythu Congress Party, or YSRCP. The party alleged that violence and threats had prevented several of its candidates from filing nomination papers for elections to around 100 urban local bodies.
The bench directed the state election commission to consider complaints submitted by the YSRCP and other candidates, along with supporting material, and decide by Thursday whether to extend the nomination deadline. It also asked the commission to take all necessary steps to address concerns among the YSRCP and other candidates about free and fair elections in the state.
The court directed the Andhra Pradesh Director General of Police to provide adequate security to candidates and election offices. It observed that the filing of nomination papers was an essential part of free and fair elections.
The bench clarified that it was not directly intervening in the election process but was allowing the state election commission to consider the party's complaint and take an appropriate decision. It asked the commission to file a compliance affidavit by October 27, the next date of hearing.
According to PTI, the court said the YS Jagan Mohan Reddy-led party had "made out prima facie case" that several of its candidates had been stopped from filing nomination papers. The court referred to representations submitted by the party and its candidates, both physically and electronically, as well as video clips and other electronic evidence.
"Bearing in mind these principles and the materials placed before us, which include various representations made by the petitioner-party as well as the candidates before the SEC both physically and in electronic form, as well as electronic evidence in the form of video clippings, etc., we are of the opinion that the petitioner has made out a prima facie case for passing the directions," the bench recorded in its order.

points: Reforming the United Nations aims to make it more effective, representative, transparent, and responsive to 21st-century realities.

sum.text:
Reforming the United Nations (UN) is one of the most critical and complex challenges in global governance today. While the UN remains indispensable, its structure, particularly its most powerful bodies, often fails to reflect the realities of the 21st century.
UN reforms refer to proposed and ongoing changes meant to make the United Nations more effective, representative, transparent, and responsive to current global realities.
The calls for reform span core UN organs, especially the Security Council, as well as the organization’s operational and financial structures.
Lack of equitable representation : The UN Security Council does not adequately reflect the current geopolitical and economic realities, particularly the growing role of developing countries. Countries like India, Brazil, Germany, and Japan, and regions such as Africa and Latin America, have long called for permanent representation to reflect modern realities and give a greater voice to developing nations. For e.g. India, despite being the world’s most populous country, does not have permanent membership in the Security Council.
Outdated Power Structure: The UN Security Council (UNSC) is dominated by five permanent members (P5: US, UK, France, Russia, China) with veto powers – a structure set in 1945 that now fails to reflect shifts in global power, the rise of developing nations, and the interests of the Global South.
Veto power of permanent members : The veto power of the five permanent members (P5) can obstruct collective action, even when a majority of countries support a resolution. Inability to address emerging global challenges : The UN’s existing institutional mechanisms often struggle to respond effectively to emerging challenges such as climate change, cyber threats, pandemics and artificial intelligence, highlighting the need for stronger international cooperation and institutional reforms. Compromised intermediate certificates allow malicious actors to issue unauthorised, spoofed SSL/TLS certificates for any website domain.
Tech conglomerates including Google, Apple, Microsoft, and Mozilla instituted immediate revocation measures across their browsers and operating systems.
Global network providers like Cloudflare deployed automated mitigations to protect underlying traffic networks from impersonation attacks.

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has constituted a specialised investigation team following disclosures regarding a security incident in eMudhra’s Public Key Infrastructure (PKI). The development follows public revelations that eight intermediate Certificate Authority (CA) certificates issued under eMudhra’s global web-security banner were compromised due to cryptographic weaknesses in their private keys.
While central authorities have assured that the operational impact on Indian applications and government portals remains minimal and short-lived, the incident has drawn global attention across cybersecurity and web infrastructure domains.
The vulnerability, initially flagged by independent security researchers, exposed eight intermediate certificates containing private keys that lacked proper cryptographic randomness during generation. Flawed key-generation algorithms made the private keys mathematically easy to derive. In digital trust architectures, intermediate certificates authorise servers to establish encrypted connections; compromising their private keys allows malicious actors to issue unauthorised, spoofed SSL/TLS certificates for any website domain.
In response to the vulnerability , tech conglomerates including Google, Apple, Microsoft, and Mozilla instituted immediate revocation measures across their respective browsers and operating systems to prevent potential impersonation attacks or traffic interception. Global network providers like Cloudflare also deployed automated mitigations to protect underlying traffic networks.
Addressing public concern, MeitY confirmed that its special investigative task force is examining the origin and extent of the key generation flaw. However, officials emphasised a clear distinction between eMudhra’s international web-security business and its domestic operations.
The ministry clarified that core domestic services—including Digital Signature Certificates (DSC) and eSign frameworks regulated directly by the Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA)—remain uncompromised. points: India has made major progress in indigenous digital infrastructure but remains dependent on foreign-controlled technologies across critical sectors like satellite communication, navigation, cloud computing, and defence.
External risks stem not only from deliberate restrictions or sanctions by foreign governments and companies, but also from technical software failures and foreign management systems.
In satellite communication, firms like Starlink, Eutelsat OneWeb, and Jio require security clearances, with foreign entities retaining ownership and control over the underlying satellite networks.
India's NavIC navigation system remains vulnerable because only three functional satellites were available for PNT signals, forcing continued reliance on the US GPS system.
Foreign hyperscale providers like AWS, Microsoft, and Google dominate cloud infrastructure, and even government MeghRaj 2.0 deployments using AWS Outposts rely on foreign regional control systems.
While India's UPI provides domestic payment autonomy, consumer-facing apps like Google Pay and PhonePe remain foreign-controlled, and cross-border transactions depend on the SWIFT network.

India remains the world's second-largest arms importer during 2021-2025, depending on Russia, France, Israel, and the US, with indigenous Tejas fighter jets facing delays due to US-made GE engine shortages.

To achieve genuine technological self-reliance, India must strengthen ISRO's launch capacity, expand domestic cloud and management systems, accelerate indigenous defence production, and enforce rigorous resilience testing.

The risk is not limited to deliberate restrictions by foreign governments or companies; technical failures, software disruptions and dependence on foreign management systems can also affect national security and economic stability.
India has licensed Starlink, Eutelsat OneWeb’s Indian subsidiary and Jio Satellite Communications to provide satellite communication services, but the article states that none had received the required security clearance for commercial satellite broadband as of October 16, 2026.
SpaceX controls Starlink, while Eutelsat OneWeb is effectively controlled by European interests and Jio’s partnership with SES does not give Jio control over the satellite network.
However, India’s dependence is limited because most ordinary telephone and internet traffic travels through terrestrial networks, while ISRO’s communication satellites and dedicated military satellites support broadcasting and strategic communications.
India’s NavIC system is particularly vulnerable because only three satellites were reported to be capable of providing positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) signals, whereas at least four are required for standalone positioning.
India therefore remains exposed to foreign navigation systems such as the US GPS, which retains the ability to deny military PNT services over specific areas.
ISRO’s difficulties in improving its launch rate have also affected NavIC’s operational reliability.
Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud provide infrastructure and managed services to thousands of Indian businesses and public institutions. Gartner projected Indian expenditure on cloud services to reach $17.5 billion in 2026.

sum.text:
With the US midterm elections approaching on November 3, President Donald Trump is facing a dilemma: can a diesel deal with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, help lower fuel prices and end the Ukraine war, or is his outreach to Moscow becoming a political liability for Republicans?
The US president’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel supplies has brought that dilemma into sharp focus. Trump is seeking to address high fuel costs at home while keeping diplomatic channels open with the Kremlin. But the concessions have triggered bipartisan criticism, strained Washington’s relationship with Kyiv and raised doubts about whether Putin is prepared to make meaningful compromises to end the war.

sum.text:
The Union Cabinet has approved the continuation of the National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) for five years, from 2026-27 to 2030-31, with a total outlay of ₹53,428 crore. The programme has been renamed the Pradhan Mantri Samajik Sahayata Yojana, with revised eligibility criteria and enhanced financial assistance under its disability pension component.
Approved on October 14, 2026, the decision aims to strengthen social security for vulnerable sections of society, including senior citizens, widows, persons with disabilities and families facing the loss of their primary breadwinner. While the old-age pension, widow pension and family benefit schemes will continue in their existing forms, the disability pension has undergone significant changes in eligibility, financial assistance and beneficiary coverage.
Launched on August 15, 1995, the National Social Assistance Programme is a centrally sponsored welfare programme that provides financial support to eligible households below the poverty line. It gives effect to Article 41 of the Constitution, which directs the State to provide public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement, within the limits of its economic capacity and development.
The programme provides 100 per cent central assistance under its components and covers both rural and urban areas. Its implementation is primarily handled by State and Union Territory administrations through designated welfare departments, with Gram Panchayats and urban local bodies also involved in identifying beneficiaries. Payments are largely made through Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT).
Under the revised nomenclature, the four components have been renamed the Pradhan Mantri Vridhavastha Pension Yojana for old-age pensions, Pradhan Mantri Vidhawa Pension Yojana for widow pensions, Pradhan Mantri Divyangjan Pension Yojana for disability pensions, and Pradhan Mantri Parivar Labh Yojana for family benefits.
The programme covered approximately 3.09 crore beneficiaries earlier, with the October 2026 approval putting the total coverage at 3.20 crore beneficiaries across all 36 States and Union Territories. The new framework retains the existing structure of three pension schemes and one family benefit scheme, while introducing wider eligibility under the disability pension.
The most significant reform concerns the disability pension, which was introduced in February 2009 as the Indira Gandhi National Disability Pension Scheme.

More significantly, the MPC shifted its policy stance from “neutral” to “calibrated tightening” — signalling that rate cuts are off the table in the near term, with future action limited to hikes or pauses. The minutes reveal sharp internal debate over how aggressively to respond to broadening inflationary pressures.

Rupee depreciation, raising import costs. FY27 inflation forecast revised upward: headline inflation to 5.2% (from 5%), core inflation to 4.4%. The world is set to breach the critical 1.5-degree temperature limit, with Donald Trump's US withdrawal from climate action worsening the outlook, according to a UN report. But there is a small silver lining.
For over a decade, scientists have warned the world must limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) to avoid the most severe consequences of climate change.
Decades of "insufficient" action on cutting the fossil fuel emissions heating the planet means overshooting 1.5-degree temperature threshold is now "imminent and unavoidable," according to the United Nations Environment Program's (UNEP) annual Emissions Gap Report.
If current climate policies continue, temperatures will rise by an average of 2.8 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels within this century. But even if countries meet their new climate pledges, global warming is still projected to reach 2.6 degrees Celsius. Both scenarios would tip the world into a period of catastrophic weather extremes.
The projections reflect a gap between what governments promise to do and the action they are taking to curb emissions. Some 167 countries have submitted climate action plans to the UN, covering 83% of global greenhouse gas emissions. But those pledges to cut emissions fall far short of what is needed to limit warming.
Among the world's largest emitters, Indonesia, China and the United States saw emissions rise in 2025, according to preliminary estimates. The increase in the US "far exceeded that of all other countries," driven by a resurgence of coal — the dirtiest fossil fuel source — and rising electricity demand, partly linked to massive AI data center expansion.

Since Trump entered the Oval Office for a second time, his administration has taken a sledgehammer to climate policy, gutting environmental regulations and expanding oil and gas production.
"The main takeaway is simple — governments need to get on with enacting policies that cut fossil fuel use as soon as possible," said Bill Hare, CEO of the global science and policy institute Climate Analytics, of the report.

Telecommunications (Regulatory Sandbox) Rules, 2026: The Central Government has notified the Telecommunications (Regulatory Sandbox) Rules, 2026, allowing eligible startups, companies, researchers and individuals to test new telecom technologies, services and business models in a controlled regulatory environment. The rules, notified by the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) under the Ministry of Communications on October 21, 2026, came into effect on the date of their publication in the Official Gazette.
The new framework, introduced under the Telecommunications Act, 2023, provides for the creation of regulatory sandboxes where innovative telecom products, networks, equipment and technologies can be tested with specified regulatory exemptions.
Who can apply under the new telecom rules?
According to the notification, eligible applicants include authorised telecom entities, companies, societies, partnership firms, statutory bodies, Indian citizens and research and development institutions recognised by the Department of Science and Technology.
Applicants can submit proposals to the government, along with reports of preliminary testing conducted in laboratory environments or experimental isolated networks.
Each proposal must be accompanied by a non-refundable processing fee of Rs 10,000.
The government can approve or reject applications after examining their eligibility.
Under the new rules, the government may grant exemptions from certain authorisation, spectrum assignment and other regulatory requirements under the Telecommunications Act, 2023, and applicable provisions under the TRAI Act, 1997.
However, exemptions relating to the applicability of provisions under the TRAI Act require prior consultation with the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India.
A regulatory sandbox can initially operate for a maximum of 24 months. The government may extend its validity by up to 12 months at a time, subject to specified conditions.
The notification also introduces safeguards for individuals participating in telecom technology trials.
Companies and other approved applicants must obtain prior consent from test users and inform them about the purpose and scope of the testing.
Importantly, test users cannot be charged for participating in the testing environment.
Approved applicants must also comply with applicable data protection and security laws.

sum.text:
Growing geopolitical tensions, increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) and risks emerging from non-bank financial institutions have raised fresh concerns over global financial stability, policymakers and experts highlighted during the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI) two-day SAMVAD 2026 seminar in New Delhi.
According to a series of posts shared by the RBI on social media platform X, discussions at the seminar focused on strengthening financial systems, managing emerging risks and ensuring that technological innovation does not undermine financial stability.
During a panel discussion on financial stability, RBI Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta observed that financial stability has become a policy objective in its own right, with the focus shifting from individual financial institutions to the broader financial system, including non-banking entities. The RBI's post noted that participants highlighted the need to remain vigilant as "crises were now coming quicker and were more intense."
The discussions also stressed the importance of addressing risks arising from climate change, financial technology companies, increasing use of AI agents and geopolitical fragmentation. Former RBI Governor and Principal Secretary-2 to the Prime Minister, Shaktikanta Das, also cautioned against emerging financial vulnerabilities linked to artificial intelligence. Das highlighted how prolonged conflicts and growing global fragmentation were tightening financial conditions and increasing sovereign debt stress. He also warned that untested AI valuations and uncertainty over profitability could increase financial vulnerabilities, while calling for stronger financial institutions, adequate financial buffers and improved regulatory supervision.
Meanwhile, Department of Economic Affairs Secretary Anuradha Thakur highlighted India's relatively strong position amid global uncertainty. She stressed that India faces the challenging global environment from a "position of macroeconomic stability", supported by a credible fiscal trajectory and flexible inflation targeting.
The seminar also examined the future of digital payments, particularly challenges surrounding AI-driven transactions and cross-border payment systems. The RBI said discussions on payment systems highlighted the importance of "access, affordability, security, speed, convenience and interoperability." Participants also emphasised common standards for cross-border transactions, stronger safeguards against financial crimes…

An estimated 47.5 million hectares, or approximately 30%, of India’s 160 million hectares of cropland should be technically suitable for agrivoltaics—where solar panels are installed directly above existing farms, Union minister for new and renewable energy (MNRE) Pralhad Joshi said on Wednesday at the inauguration of the 7th edition of the AgriVoltaics World Conference (AWC) 2026 in Delhi’s Bharat Mandapam. One deployment scenario covering 16 million hectares estimates annual electricity generation of 12,775 TWh, potentially comparable to or exceeding India’s projected electricity demand of 5,250–10,020 TWh by 2050,” said Joshi, stating one of the world’s most ambitious agrivoltaic programmes would be launched under the next phase of PM-Kusum.“Elevated and tilted structures could make agrivoltaic plants 25–30% more expensive than conventional ground-mounted solar installations, and the government aims to bridge this cost gap by supporting AgriPV capacity creation,” the minister added.
The conference was inaugurated alongside the agriculture minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan too, who said any AgriPV policy must be designed to meet the practical requirements of India’s small and marginal farmers, who constitute more than 85% of the farming community. Currently, coverage of ground-mounted solar panels is part of the existing PM Kusum scheme, which provides subsidies to farmers for both ground-mounted panels and solar pumps.“The average landholding in the country is only 0.96 hectares. Thus, agrivoltaics models must allow farmers to continue cultivation instead of replacing farming with solar power generation,” Chouhan said.

static: The Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, regulate digital news, social media intermediaries, and OTT platforms in India.
Intermediaries are entities that store or transmit data on behalf of third parties, enjoying statutory safe harbor protections under Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000.
The principles of natural justice are non-statutory principles of fairness, including the right to a fair hearing (audi alteram partem) and the rule against bias.
Article 21 of the Constitution guarantees that no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law, which must be fair and reasonable.

points: The Punjab and Haryana High Court held that informing a user is an essential requirement under natural justice when blocking social media pages.
The ruling came in a petition by Haryana 24 News Network Private Limited after Meta blocked its page following a police order.
Justice Tribhuvan Dahiya noted that the IT Act and 2021 Rules do not explicitly mandate a pre-decisional hearing, but users are directly affected.
The court stated that a post-decisional hearing before a grievance officer is meaningless unless the user knows about the action and the government's reasons.
The bench read the obligation to furnish a copy of the government intimation to the affected user into Rule 3(2) of the 2021 Rules.
The court also ruled that the Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP), Yamunanagar, was not authorised to issue the blocking order.
The rules prescribe that the authorised officer must be of a rank not below that of an Inspector General of Police (IGP).

sum.text:
The court held that informing the user is an essential requirement under the principles of natural justice, even though the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, do not explicitly prescribe such an obligation.
The ruling came in a petition filed by Haryana 24 News Network Private Limited, a news platform operating in Haryana, which approached the high court after Meta blocked its social media page in India on August 21, following an order issued by Haryana Police.
Justice Tribhuvan Dahiya, who presided over the matter, observed that although the Information Technology Act, 2000, and the rules framed under it do not provide for a hearing to the affected user before the government issues a blocking intimation to the intermediary, the user is directly affected by the resulting restriction on access to their online content or page.
The court noted that the issue of providing prior notice to a user before blocking a social media page was not under consideration in the present case. However, the question of providing a post-decisional hearing before the platform’s grievance officer was relevant to the dispute.
The bench observed that such a hearing would be meaningful only if the affected user had knowledge of the action taken against them, including the contents of the government’s intimation and the material relied upon to issue it.
“In its absence, he cannot defend himself and the very purpose of providing the grievance redressal mechanism under the rule gets defeated,” the court observed.
Emphasising the importance of procedural fairness, the high court stated that every procedure established by law must be fair and reasonable and must comply with the basic principles of natural justice, including the right to a fair hearing.
The court acknowledged that sub-rule (2) of Rule 3 of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, does not expressly require the government or its agency to notify the person responsible for uploading the information before sending a blocking intimation to the intermediary.
However, the bench held that such an obligation is inherent in the principles of natural justice and must be read into the rule.
Accordingly, the court ruled that a copy of the government’s intimation must be furnished to the affected user at the time it is sent to the social media intermediary.

explain.headline: Supreme Court Rules Pre-Trial Detention Cannot Become Punishment Without Trial
static: Article 21 of the Constitution guarantees the right to life and personal liberty, which the Supreme Court has repeatedly interpreted to include the right to a speedy trial.

Bail is a judicial remedy meant to ensure the presence of the accused during trial while upholding the cardinal principle of criminal jurisprudence that an accused is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

Under the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) or Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), prolonged detention during investigation or trial serves as a key ground for granting bail when delays are not attributable to the accused.
The Jal Jeevan Mission is a flagship central scheme aimed at providing safe and adequate drinking water through individual household tap connections to all rural households in India.
explain.what: The Supreme Court granted regular bail to two accused in a corruption case, ruling that prolonged pre-trial detention cannot become punishment without trial and violates Article 21.
explain.why_in_news: The Supreme Court made this observation while granting regular bail to former Congress minister Mahesh Chandra Joshi and Mukesh Pathak in a Jal Jeevan Mission corruption case.
explain.background: The Court balanced the gravity of financial corruption allegations with the fundamental right to a speedy trial, noting that completed investigations and delayed trials render continued pre-trial detention unjustified.
significance: Reinforces the constitutional principle that 'bail is the rule and jail is the exception' even in serious economic offences.
Highlights systemic delays in the Indian criminal justice system involving voluminous documents and numerous witnesses.
Emphasises that pre-trial detention must not be used as a substitute for punitive sentencing.
prelims: Mahesh Chandra Joshi and Mukesh Pathak were granted regular bail by the Supreme Court.
The case involves alleged irregularities in tenders worth hundreds of crores under the Jal Jeevan Mission in Rajasthan.
The case features 22 accused persons, three chargesheets, 124 prosecution witnesses, and 192 documents running into 20,000 pages.
Mahesh Chandra Joshi was in jail from May 7, 2026, and Mukesh Pathak from February 18, 2026.
explain.mains: Examine the judicial principles governing pre-trial detention in India. How does prolonged incarceration without trial infringe upon the fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution?
explain.who: Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu, Mahesh Chandra Joshi, Mukesh Pathak
explain.video_query: Supreme Court pre-trial detention speedy trial judgment explained

stories.ai_why: Important Supreme Court observation on pre-trial detention and personal liberty.

points: The Supreme Court ruled that prolonged pre-trial detention cannot become punishment without trial, protecting personal liberty and speedy trial rights under Article 21.
The observation was made by a bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu while granting regular bail in a corruption case linked to the Jal Jeevan Mission.
The Court stated that the seriousness of allegations regarding large-scale financial irregularities cannot alone justify keeping an accused in custody indefinitely.
The investigation against appellants Mahesh Chandra Joshi and Mukesh Pathak was complete and chargesheets had been filed.
The prosecution evidence relied on documents and electronic records already secured by investigators, removing the need for further custodial interrogation or recovery.
Joshi had been in jail for over five months since May 7, 2026, and Pathak for nearly eight months since February 18, 2026, without the trial beginning.
The case involves 22 accused, 3 chargesheets, 124 witnesses, and around 20,000 pages of evidence, indicating the trial would take considerable time.
The appellants had already secured bail in connected proceedings, and several co-accused had also received bail or interim protection.
The Supreme Court concluded that further incarceration was unnecessary and any prosecution concerns could be addressed through appropriate bail conditions.
sum.text:
New Delhi, October 22, 2026: The Supreme Court has ruled that prolonged detention before trial cannot become a form of punishment, stressing that the right to personal liberty and a speedy trial must be protected even in cases involving serious allegations of financial irregularities. A bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu made the observation while granting regular bail to former Congress minister Mahesh Chandra Joshi and Mukesh Pathak in a corruption case linked to alleged irregularities in tenders worth hundreds of crores of rupees under the Jal Jeevan Mission in Rajasthan, Live Law reported. Serious Allegations Cannot Justify Indefinite DetentionThe Court said allegations of large-scale financial irregularities and collusion in a public welfare project were serious and required thorough scrutiny.
However, it made clear that the seriousness of the allegations alone could not justify keeping a person in custody indefinitely without trial.“As repeatedly emphasised by this Court, prolonged pre-trial detention cannot be permitted to degenerate into punishment without trial in derogation of an undertrial’s Fundamental Right to personal liberty and speedy trial guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution,” the Court observed. The bench acknowledged that the State was justified in opposing bail in cases involving extensive alleged criminal activity. However, it stressed that courts must consider other factors before deciding whether continued detention is necessary.
The ruling reinforces the principle that serious allegations cannot override an undertrial’s constitutional rights. Evidence Already With InvestigatorsThe Court noted that the investigation against Joshi and Pathak had been completed and chargesheets had been filed. The prosecution’s case was largely based on documents and electronic evidence already in the custody of the investigating agency.
The evidence included tender files, official correspondence, bank statements, forensic reports of seized mobile phones and intercepted conversations. The bench found that neither further custodial interrogation nor recovery was required from the two appellants, substantially reducing concerns about possible tampering with evidence. Months In Jail, Trial Yet To BeginThe Court also considered the time both appellants had already spent in custody.
Joshi, aged about 72, had been in jail since May 7, 2026, for more than five months, while Pathak had remained in continuous custody since February 18,…

Patients and caregivers cannot demand the procedure clinically, though participation in approved clinical trials remains permitted without therapeutic misconception.

Medical practitioners offering it as a clinical service outside regulated settings fail to meet the reasonable standard of care owed to patients.</p><p>“In such circumstances, the individuals diagnosed with ASD, or their parents/guardians/caregivers cannot demand that such a form of procedure be permitted to be administered as a clinical service," the bench said.</p>.Stem cell therapy in India: NMC tightens rules, bars use for unproven treatments.<p>However, participation in an approved research or clinical trial remains open, provided participants are free of “therapeutic misconception” — the mistaken belief that the primary purpose is treatment rather than research, the court said.</p><p>The <a href="https://www.deccanherald.com/tags/supreme-court">Supreme Court</a> also clarified that its January 30, 2026, judgment does not impose an immutable ban. Should rigorous, regulated research later establish safety, efficacy and ethical acceptability, competent authorities may reconsider permitting the intervention under appropriate conditions, it said.</p><p>Research involving stem cells with more than minimal manipulation falls under the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) and the New Drugs and Clinical Trial Rules, 2019.

sum.text:
Dehradun, Oct 22 (PTI) Uttarakhand Cabinet approved 25 proposals as it met on Thursday, ahead of the two-day Assembly session scheduled to take place in the winter capital Gairsain next week.
The proposals approved included changes in the Uniform Civil Code Rules, a one-time settlement scheme for resolution of pending stamp-duty-related cases, and establishment of an Uttarakhand Adventure Tourism Corporation Limited.
The cabinet meeting, chaired by Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami, also approved changes to the approval process for road and bridge construction works under the Public Works Department.
Currently, under the second phase, approvals for various components -- such as hill-slope cutting, construction of retaining walls, culverts, drains and other related works -- are granted in separate stages.
As per the new system, all works in the second phase will be approved in a single stage, which will ensure that all essential protective measures after hill-slope cutting can be implemented in a timely manner, thereby minimising damage to the roads.
The cabinet also approved a proposal to raise the annual family income limit for eligibility under the free coaching scheme to Rs 8 lakh from Rs 2 lakh.
The scheme is run by the Social Welfare Department for students belonging to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. Officials said the new approval will enable a larger number of students to avail free coaching for competitive examinations.
Approval was also given to notify the "Civil Code (Amendment) Rules, Uttarakhand, 2026" to implement the provisions of the "Uniform Civil Code, Uttarakhand (Amendment) Act, 2026".
Officials said this will address the practical difficulties encountered during the implementation of certain provisions of the original Code, and also rectify clerical errors.
The meeting also gave nod to amendments to the relevant regulations, to grant 5 per cent relaxation in passing marks for students with disabilities appearing for examinations conducted by the Uttarakhand Board of School Education.
Consequently, students falling under this category will be considered "passed" upon securing 28 per cent marks.
In the cabinet meeting, a decision was taken to restructure all 13 District Institutes of Education and Training (DIET) in the state, through which the number of existing positions in each DIET will be reduced from 48 to 44.
Under the "PM Poshan" scheme, the cabinet approved a proposal to allocate land to Annamrita Foundation in Haridwar…

points: The Tadoba-Andhari Tiger Reserve in Maharashtra has introduced a sensor-based system on a pilot basis to regulate wildlife waterhole water levels.
The initiative addresses the problem of solar-powered pumps continuing to operate after waterholes are full, causing water overflow and excessive groundwater extraction.

TATR Field Director Dr Prabhu Nath Shukla stated the device automatically starts and stops pumps based on predefined lower and upper water level limits.

sum.text:
Chandrapur, The Tadoba-Andhari Tiger Reserve in Maharashtra's Chandrapur district has introduced a sensor-based system on a pilot basis to regulate water levels at wildlife waterholes, reduce wastage and ensure reliable water availability for animals, officials said. Describing it as a first-of-its-kind initiative in wildlife waterhole management, TATR Field Director Dr Prabhu Nath Shukla said the device automatically starts and stops pumps based on water levels. The system activates the pump when the water level falls below a predefined limit and switches it off once the water reaches the upper level, preventing overflow and unnecessary pumping, he said in a release issued on Wednesday.
The initiative comes at a time when drought conditions and uncertainty over future water availability have made efficient water management increasingly important. TATR has around 130 natural water sources and 350 artificial waterholes, many of which are supported by solar-powered pumping systems. Despite last summer's intense heat, no water tankers were required to refill these waterholes, the release said.
However, solar-powered pumps often continue to operate even after waterholes are full, leading to overflow. While some excess water serves as wallowing spots for wild animals, manually switching off the pumps can be risky for staff and is not an efficient solution. Shukla said the sensor-based system would help reduce water loss, limit unnecessary groundwater extraction and minimise the need for continuous human monitoring.
The device comprises a level sensor, controller and relay connected to the pump. It functions automatically, ensuring water availability while reducing manual intervention, he added." TATR is presenting the system as a first-of-its-kind sensor-based approach to wildlife waterhole management. Its wider use could strengthen water conservation, help the management in providing water availability to the wildlife even during drought conditions, and also aid groundwater conservation," said Shukla.
To improve the spatial distribution of water sources across the reserve, TATR has divided its core area into grids and plans to provide waterholes in each grid. The exercise, aimed at ensuring equitable access to water for wildlife across the reserve, is expected to be completed this year, the release said. sum.text: CHANDIGARH: Union Agriculture and Farmers Welfare Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan on Thursday launched a nationwide campaign to promote sustainable farming, improve soil health and encourage judicious use of resources. Through the 'Khet Bachao Abhiyan --Rabi 2026', which was launched from Taraori in Karnal district, the government seeks to strengthen soil and water conservation, promote efficient and cost-effective farming practices, improve agricultural sustainability and contribute to the long-term prosperity of farmers and the vision of 'Viksit Bharat'. Addressing farmers, agricultural scientists, and officials, who joined virtually from Krishi Vigyan Kendras and various agricultural institutions across the country, the Union minister warned that if the imbalanced use of chemical fertilizers and pesticides is not halted, the soil will eventually lose its ability to produce crops. He further cautioned that it will also have an impact on human health. Commending Haryana farmers for their efforts in stubble management, Chouhan stated that burning stubble in fields not only cause air pollution but also destroys microorganisms, beneficial insects, and earthworms, which act as natural soil enrichers, residing in the upper and lower layers of the soil. Nearly all of the world's shallow-water coral reefs face an "extremely high risk" of collapse by 2075 due to climate change, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) warned Thursday.
In the first global assessment of its kind, the world authority on threatened wildlife classified 96 percent of the planet's coral reef systems as "critically endangered" -- its highest risk category.
Corals are heat sensitive and particularly vulnerable to human-driven climate change, which is warming the world's oceans and increasing the frequency and intensity of damaging bleaching events.
"The risk of coral reef collapse is escalating, but this must be a wake-up call rather than a cause for despair," said Mishal Gudka, scientific lead of the IUCN Red List of Coral Reef Ecosystems assessment.
"Coral reefs have shown a remarkable ability to bounce back from devastating bleaching events," said Gudka, who is also research director at Coastal Oceans Research and Development in the Indian Ocean (CORDIO) East Africa, a conservation organisation.
For their assessment, researchers used the "middle-of-the-road" scenario from the UN's panel of climate experts that projects global temperatures rising 2.7C above pre-industrial levels by 2100.
The world is on track for 2.6C warming this century under current global commitments to cut planet-heating emissions, the United Nations warned Wednesday.
"Heat stress from climate change is the single most consistent threat driving coral reef decline worldwide," the IUCN said in a statement.
Overfishing is also hurting corals as certain herbivores and predators help control algae and maintain an ecological balance, the organisation said.
The overexploitation of parrotfish and other groupers threatens 63 percent of coral reef ecosystems.
Coastal development, pollution, tourism and more frequent storms are among other threats.
The IUCN's analysis examined 127 tropical and subtropical coral systems covering 188,362 square kilometres.
The world's largest and most biodiverse coral reefs are among those classified as critically endangered -- Australia's Great Barrier Reef, the Coral Triangle in southeast Asia and the western Pacific, the Caribbean's Mesoamerican Barrier Reef System, and the Red Sea coral reefs.
A reef ecosystem collapses when hard corals -- which build its living foundation -- largely disappear and are replaced by algae, rubble and sponges.

India has strongly rejected a United Nations special rapporteur's description of fugitive gangster Dawood Ibrahim's D-Company as an “India-based” criminal group, citing “glaring inaccuracies” in a counter-terrorism report. India said such factual errors and the lack of accountability for UN experts could undermine the credibility of the world body. It maintained that Ibrahim had fled India long before his 2003 listing by the UN Security Council for his association with Al-Qaeda and Osama bin Laden.
Raghoo Puri, First Secretary at India's Permanent Mission to the UN, raised the objections on Wednesday during a meeting of the Third Committee of the UN General Assembly. He was responding to a report by Ben Saul, the Special Rapporteur on the promotion and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms while countering terrorism.“My delegation has been pointing out in other forums as well our serious concern at the unacceptable situation of the SR (Special Rapporteur) releasing reports with factual inaccuracies, while not being held accountable for them,” Puri said. He described this as an unfortunate situation for an organisation already facing challenges to its legitimacy. According to news agency ANI, Puri said, “It is in this context that we would like to point out some particularly glaring inaccuracies as far as my country is concerned.” Puri objected to Saul's report stating that the UN Security Council had in 2003 listed the leader of one criminal group, “the India-based D-Company”, for association with Al-Qaeda.“Read in isolation, this line paints a very different picture from the actual reality,” Puri said, strongly rejecting the description of the criminal organisation as India-based. He said D-Company and its listed leader, Dawood Ibrahim, had been wanted in India in connection with terror attacks since 1993.
He added that this was documented in the narrative summary explaining the reasons for Ibrahim's listing under the UN Security Council's 1267 Al-Qaeda sanctions regime.“This is clearly written in the narrative summary of reasons of listing under the 1267 sanctions regime,” Puri said. CORSIA is a global market-based mechanism adopted by the International Civil Aviation Organization in 2016 to reduce carbon emissions from international flights.
Under the scheme, airlines compensate for their international flight CO2 emissions by purchasing eligible carbon offsets.
Airlines operating international flights between participating states must monitor, report, and verify CO2 emissions and purchase offsets for emissions growth above a baseline.

sum.text:
Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation Latest News With just over two months remaining before CORSIA’s mandatory phase kicks in, India is yet to finalise a comprehensive national Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) policy. About Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation It is a global market-based mechanism to reduce carbon emissions from international flights. It was adopted by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) in 2016.
It is the first global market-based measure for any industry sector. Under CORSIA, airlines compensate for their international flight’s CO₂ emissions by purchasing carbon offsets. A carbon offset is a credit for carbon reductions made by one party that can be purchased to compensate for the emissions generated by another party.
Under CORSIA, airlines operating international flights between participating states must monitor, report, and verify (MRV) their CO₂ emissions, and purchase eligible emissions units (offsets) to compensate for growth in emissions above an established baseline. Originally the baseline was set as the average of 2019 and 2020 emissions, but in 2020 the ICAO Council adjusted the baseline to 2019-only levels to prevent the COVID-19 collapse in air travel from making the scheme unduly stringent. CORSIA only applies to international flights.
Domestic emissions fall under the scope of the UNFCCC and are covered by the Paris Agreement. The scheme runs in phases: A pilot phase (2021–2023) and first phase (2024–2026), both voluntary, in which roughly 120+ states have volunteered. A mandatory phase (2027-2035), covering all ICAO member states except those exempted (least developed countries, small island developing states, landlocked developing countries, and states with very small shares of international aviation activity).
Compliance reports covering 2024‑2026 emissions are due to national authorities by 31 January 2028. Such offsets can be sourced from various types of activities, including, for example, the deployment of renewable energy, clean cooking technologies, methane capture, forestry, and other emissions-reducing projects.

Published by German aid agency Welthungerhilfe (WHH) and Irish organisation Concern Worldwide, the index measures hunger and undernutrition across countries and tracks progress and setbacks. The 2026 edition draws on data from 2021 to 2025.
The GHI uses a 100-point scale, with lower scores indicating less hunger. Scores from 10 to 19.9 fall in the “moderate” category, while those from 20 to 34.9 are classified as “serious”.
India’s GHI score fell from 38.1 in 2000 to 24.1 in 2026, with 9.8 percent of the population being undernourished. More significantly, the score declined by just 1.7 points between 2018 and 2026, compared with an 8.2-point drop between 2006 and 2012.
“India's GHI score, considered serious since 2012, mirrors the regional slowdown, with the score easing from 25.8 in 2018 to 24.1 in 2026,” the report said. It added that this “represents a fraction of its steep improvement of 8.2 points between 2006 and 2012.”
The GHI is based on four indicators: undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting and child mortality.
Undernourishment fell to 9.8 percent in 2026. Child wasting, however, stood at 19 percent—the highest rate in the region—and remained high across all the reference years examined in the report. Wasting occurs when children under five weigh too little for their height and is usually a sign of acute undernutrition.
The report also accounts for factors associated with undernutrition, including poor diet quality, infections, and inadequate access to health services, safe water and sanitation.
Stunting, which reflects chronic undernutrition, fell to 29.3 percent in 2026, moving India from the “very high” to the “high” category for the first time. Child mortality also fell, with the share of children dying before their fifth birthday dropping from 9.2 percent in 2000 to 2.7 percent in 2026.

The meeting was co-chaired by Dr Suhel Ajaz Khan, Additional Secretary (Counter Terrorism) in India’s Ministry of External Affairs, and Pirimkulov Gulomjon Shodmonkulovich, a senior official of Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Discussions covered global and regional terrorist threats, including extremism, radicalisation, terrorism financing and the misuse of technology for terrorist purposes. The sides also discussed links between transnational organised crime and terrorism. The 9th meeting of the Joint Working Group took place in Tashkent on 30 September 2025. At that meeting, India and Uzbekistan condemned the 22 April 2025 terrorist attack targeting civilians in Pahalgam, Jammu and Kashmir. The next meeting is scheduled to take place in Uzbekistan on a mutually convenient date.
India and Uzbekistan reaffirmed cooperation in the United Nations, the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation’s Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (SCO-RATS), and the Eurasian Group on combating money laundering and terrorism financing. SCO-RATS is a permanent body of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation that coordinates cooperation among member states against terrorism, separatism and extremism. The Eurasian Group is a regional intergovernmental body that addresses money laundering and the financing of terrorism.
In August 2026, India and Uzbekistan elevated their bilateral relationship to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership covering defence, counter-terrorism and cybersecurity. The 7th edition of their joint military exercise, DUSTLIK 2026, was held from 12 to 25 April at the Gurumsaray Field Training Area in Uzbekistan.

Researchers from Gauhati University have identified a new flowering plant species, “ Osbeckia assamensis ”, in the grasslands of Manas National Park, Assam.
Osbeckia assamensis belongs to the Melastomataceae family and was discovered during floristic surveys conducted between 2021 and 2025 in Manas National Park. It is a perennial shrub that grows approximately 2–2.5 metres tall, with pink flowers, large opposite leaves and a largely unbranched stem. The plant flowers and bears fruit from September to February. The species grows in the grasslands of Manas National Park, located in the Himalayan foothills . Its conservation status is classified as Data Deficient (DD) under the IUCN criteria , indicating insufficient information to assess its risk of extinction.
